channel.title: sgit.ai articles
channel.description: Articles and desk notes from sgit.ai, newest first.

item.title: Legal on demand for startups: agent teams that do the reading, lawyers who sign, and a meter instead of a retainer, with three vaults that show the founder's desk, the investor's desk and the deal room
item.description: Legal advice is in every part of a startup, from shares and votes to IP and people, and most founders have little experience of it and little access to good lawyers. So they sign deals that are worse than they need to be, often with no malice on anyone's side. Legal services never scaled because the work took time, much of it repetitive, and good people did not want to do it. GenAI changes that: models are very good at reading every detail and finding inconsistencies, and an agent team can do the reading, the checking and the drafting so that a lawyer's time goes on judgement and signature. That makes a service that scales: on the founder's side, on the investor's side, and in a deal room where both teams meet, with every understanding, clause and version signed and verifiable. Paid per task or by a monthly plan, not a yearly retainer. I think someone should build it, and most of what it needs exists today in open source. To show it, three made-up vaults: Tallowmere Counsel's founder desk, investor desk and deal room, with real signatures your browser checks.

item.title: Who has not patched? How good the "unpatched" numbers for php2shell are, what makes a website actually vulnerable, and why not patching can be the rational decision
item.description: Six days after php2shell, the headlines say most websites have not patched, and the subtext is that businesses do not take security seriously. Before accepting that, ask how good the number is. Every figure published so far is a count of version strings, not of vulnerable sites; Italy's national CSIRT, the best of them, found 81.9% of PHP services whose version it could read below the fix, which is 38.5% of all it detected, and a fixed package can keep its old number. A site is only vulnerable if it is exploitable: reachable, without protection in front (Cloudflare, behind about 28% of websites, had rules live on every plan nine hours before disclosure), on a runtime the exploit fits (the public exploits need an exact build and worker), with something worth taking and nobody watching. And no named organisation has yet said it was compromised through php2shell. So the more likely explanation for "not patching" is not negligence: the count is wrong, the threat is low where it matters, and security teams are patching other things first, which is their job.

item.title: What an agent is: a session, a card, a loop and a key. How the PHP newsroom's agents now run on schedules and in one session, and what the record says about it
item.description: I have moved from many Claude sessions to agent teams that run on schedules. The PHP October 2026 newsroom is the furthest along: a pipeline of researcher, curator, journalist and correspondent runs in order five times a day, a desk twice, a conductor every hour, and eight more agents keep the house, all on their own schedule cards. For two days it has run in sequence with no content commit from me. Then there is a second way to run the same agents: in one session, as subagents, which is how the newsroom carried CISA's listing of php2shell to readers in 5 hours 21 minutes. Writing this up against the team's own record corrected me in several places: the conductor does not start the breaking run, the agents' keys seal secrets but do not yet sign their work, and nothing has run on anything but Claude. What it confirmed is the main point: an agent is a session plus a card, a role, a loop, a key and memory kept in repositories and vaults, and only the first part is the model.

item.title: Take it or leave it: is Meta's crawling clause legal? The law that could reach it, the precedents against Meta, and the asymmetry at its heart
item.description: Meta's updated Commercial Terms, due on 20 November 2026, let Meta crawl the websites of any business that uses Facebook, Instagram or WhatsApp, create test credentials on them, and keep pulling updates; a business that does not agree must stop all business use of Meta's products. My first reaction was that this is blackmail. The law has a more precise word: Article 102 of the EU Treaty, and the UK's Competition Act word for word, forbid a dominant company from making a contract conditional on "supplementary obligations" that have "no connection with the subject" of the contract. This is not legal advice, and no regulator or court has ruled on the clause. But the routes exist: competition law, which has already found Meta's terms for business customers unfair once, in 2024; the EU's Digital Markets Act; the platform-to-business rules; copyright; and, in the UK, a regulator that says it is "very alive" to the risk but has not designated Meta. And there is an asymmetry worth stating plainly: everything the clause lets Meta do to a business's website, Meta's own terms forbid on Facebook and WhatsApp. If it is legal, I think it should not be.

item.title: Meta's new terms and the news: what the crawling clause says, what has happened since mid-October, and why publishers should answer with their own machine-readable terms, not only with letters
item.description: Meta has updated the Commercial Terms that apply to any business use of Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp and its ad tools. One clause authorises Meta, or anyone acting for it, to use "web scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers and user agents" and "create test credentials" to access, cache and collect the websites associated with a business, and to pull updates periodically, to "provide, develop, improve, research and maintain advertising and business products". Almost every news organisation has a Facebook Page, so almost every news site is in scope. The terms were due on 30 October; after publishers' associations around the world objected, Meta removed the word "train", said the terms are "only" about ads and business products and that robots.txt still counts, and moved the date to 20 November. Robots.txt is not in the contract, and the price of saying no is to stop using Meta for business. Tami Hoffman, Director of Public Policy at The Guardian, explained it in a 90-second video that is filling inboxes. This is a debrief of the change and the dispute, and my view: the letters to Meta and the regulators are needed, but publishers should also act now, with machine-readable licence terms, a price per crawl, signed content, and channels they own, and we have been building and proposing exactly those.

item.title: The evidence behind four days: Jeremiah Grossman's php2shell post, checked claim by claim against the data, with the provenance and the graphs, and the two things that changed since
item.description: Four days after php2shell went public, Jeremiah Grossman, CEO of Root Evidence, posted on LinkedIn that the evidence does not support the wave of AI-enabled breaches many were bracing for, that the exploits are environment-specific, that in the same four days over a thousand CVEs were published and almost none were exploited, and that the rule is the old one: patch what adversaries exploit. This is the data behind each claim, re-counted from public sources and from the PHP story site's evidence, with every number traceable to a query or a captured source. Most of it holds. The post's timestamp is the CVE record's to the second; NVD counts 1,394 CVEs in the same window, not 1,448; none references Exploit-DB or Metasploit; VulnCheck published 25 old bugs with 2017 to 2025 IDs on 22 October; CISA had listed one, the Arista flaw. Two things changed after the post: CISA added both php2shell CVEs to its catalogue on 26 October, and their EPSS scores went from 0.06 and 0.12 to above 0.999 the day before. As of 09:43 UTC on 27 October, no named organisation had said it was compromised through php2shell. The yearly numbers are consistent with the post's wider point, but cannot test it: CVE publications more than doubled this year, while additions to CISA's catalogue rose by 30%. Corrected on 27 October after a review by ChatGPT, which the editor asked for; the changes are listed at the end.

item.title: The IPO filing and the agents: what Anthropic tells investors about the risks of its own agents, in its own words, and where RiskMandate and Agent Behaviour Policies answer each one
item.description: On 26 October 2026 Anthropic filed its registration statement for an initial public offering on Nasdaq. Its risk factors contain the most candid description of the risks of AI agents I have read from a vendor: agents with "enterprise-level permissions" running for hours or days; actions that are "difficult or impossible to reverse"; models "granting themselves permissions they had not been given"; human reviewers with "alert fatigue"; agents that "amplify, propagate, or reinforce misaligned behavior"; audit trails that are "technically challenging"; prompt injection that redirects an agent with "the customer's authenticated credentials"; and liability that is "unsettled". It even describes models that reached real third-party systems during an evaluation, "despite instructions that it had no internet access". This article quotes the ten agent risks with their page numbers, and maps each one to what RiskMandate and Agent Behaviour Policies do about it, with what we have built, tested and measured, and what is still proposed. The short version: a policy cannot make a model aligned, but it can write down what an agent may do, keep each rule somewhere the agent cannot change, and produce evidence that does not come from the agent.

item.title: What the $2,000 bitcoin bounty actually proves: php2shell's real timeline, whether a firewall could have seen it coming, and what hardening can and cannot do without the patch
item.description: A researcher won a public "steal my bitcoin" bounty against a deliberately vulnerable PHP server, a rare independent, live confirmation that php2shell gives an attacker full control of a machine. I wanted to know more than that it worked. How hard was it, really, once the target was actually reachable? Could a web application firewall have blocked it, given how many vendors say they already detect it? And if you cannot patch today, does hardening the server around PHP, rather than PHP itself, actually protect you? The answers, checked against the operator's own site, the researcher's public write-up, five vendors' own advisories and GrapheneOS's own record of a server it chose to take offline rather than trust its own mitigations: the bounty took three hours once there was a page to attack, not the nineteen the headlines reported; every vendor's own detection coverage comes with a gap it names itself; and every hardening measure anyone has published is described by its own authors as partial. Patching remains the only complete fix.

item.title: PHP October 2026, update 4: still no confirmed victim, one repository becomes six, the main site moves to the new build, and the agents get faster tools (26 October, 17:16 UTC)
item.description: The fourth update on php2shell and the newsroom covering it, as of 17:16 UTC on 26 October. Five days after the release, no named organisation has said it was compromised through php2shell; the evidence vault holds 543 sources, and the advice is moving from "install the fix" to "and check whether you were already broken into". A won "steal my bitcoin" challenge proved the flaw gives full control of a machine, on a server built to be attacked. The newsroom changed more than the story did. On 25 October the site's one repository became six, press, data, site, refs, updates and team, each with its own writers, version, gate and address; a release now goes live in 25 to 42 seconds instead of a median of 88, and a change to the references is checked in 7 seconds instead of 75. On 26 October the old repository was frozen, every agent moved to sgit 0.25.0, which cut the researcher's pass from 57 minutes to 35, the curator started writing its own data files after a written proposal, and at 17:07 UTC the main address was switched to the new build. What is not done yet: each site still waits on one build, run by hand, until a token only I can set is in place.

item.title: Websites you own: a reply to an infographic that sells AI-built websites by the month, section by section, why rent is the wrong model, and the one-off model I propose, where the client owns Claude, GitHub and the domain, and changes their own site by talking to it
item.description: Someone I am helping, who is doing a lot of agentic work now, sent me an infographic for a business selling websites built with Claude: three monthly plans from £39 to £119 with a setup fee, a cap of five or ten pages, half an hour to two hours of edits a month, the seller's Claude subscription as the main cost, and ten clients making about £570 a month. It is a good sign that people see the opportunity. But the temptation is always rent, money while you sleep, and the economics are wrong. On a monthly plan you earn most when your clients use you least, the clients who use you most cost you most, and a few of them will never stop asking. The page caps make no sense either: a static page costs almost nothing, and this newsroom runs about 1,500 of them on GitHub Pages. The model I propose is different. The client owns three accounts, Claude or ChatGPT, GitHub with Pages, and a domain. You charge once, to set them up and wire them together, build the site from the client's own material with designs to choose from, check it, and hand it over with a lesson in changing it by talking to their AI. After that, help is a block of hours, if they want it. Every engagement ends, the client is in control, and delighted clients tell others. Here is the infographic, section by section, and the alternative.

item.title: Inside Kitewing Websites: a made-up studio that sells websites you own, and three made-up client sites built as vault apps, a potter's catalogue, a community garden and a local plumber's guides library, each one file, each different, and each ready to be changed by talking to it
item.description: To make the model in websites you own concrete, the agents built a mock-up of it. Kitewing Websites is a made-up studio that sells exactly that offer: setup of three accounts the client owns, a build from the client's own material with designs to choose from, QA, a handover, and nothing monthly. Next to it are three made-up client sites in a made-up town called Harrowby, chosen because they are the kinds of site that sound complicated and are easy for an agent to maintain: Tidewrack Studio Pottery, a catalogue of 28 pieces with filters; Fennick Lane Community Garden, with a season of events, a volunteer rota and 14 growing guides; and Quillon Heat & Plumbing, a local trade with a map of the villages it covers and 19 household guides. Each is one HTML file with its words and data in a JSON file beside it, no external requests, no fonts or images to fetch, and each looks different. They are built as vault apps, so each can live in an encrypted sgit vault, and the studio's vault holds the three examples inside it: a vault in a vault. The four vaults are pushed and published with their public read keys, and the four sites are also served here, as previews.

item.title: One researcher for every newsroom: a research site that works as a light, focused Internet Archive for the sources our stories rest on, captured on a schedule into a pack a day, published by licence tier, and shared by the PHP site, the wires and the Web Summit newsroom
item.description: Every newsroom we run has its own researcher. The PHP story site's source watch re-reads about 900 pages from some 600 publishers, the Industry Wire reads its own sources, and the Web Summit newsroom will need the same. That is a lot of repeated work, and it is slow: a full watch pass takes 16 to 27 minutes for a few hundred pages, before the commit and the push. Now that we know how to run agents on a schedule, with a conductor, a researcher and a dev team, the next step is to consolidate: one shared researcher, publishing everything it is allowed to at research.newsroom.sgit.ai, a light and very focused version of the Internet Archive. Teams declare what they want watched; scheduled runs capture it in parallel, a daily run of the general web, a run for Wikipedia, and focus runs for current stories; each day becomes one sgit pack, a zip with its commits, so the provenance travels with the data. The site makes the files easy to find, says what each holds, and lets anyone download them. What it may show is decided by the licence tiers the source watch already uses: open and public-sector pages in full, the rest as index, hashes and links. This is the design, for review before we build it.

item.title: Web Summit 2026, the plan: a briefing for the team on usage first and the sale after, intelligence from public material, an asset, a page and a link for every person we want to reach, a newsroom of our own for the summit, and the two agentic workflows the team will learn on
item.description: Web Summit runs in Lisbon from 9 to 12 November 2026, and this time we have help. There are five of us with tickets, two founders, a project manager, a Gen AI consultant and technical expert, and a Gen AI founder and explorer coder, so we can work the summit as a team. This is the briefing to align us. The main objectives are usage and the sale, in that order: the sale happens after people use what we build. Usage depends on very easy onboarding, five minutes to the value, as the RiskMandate customer site does. Around that, three parallel tracks: intelligence on who to talk to, from public material only; outreach, with messaging made for one company or one post; and content, articles and interviews that bring traffic, because only traffic and use show us where we add value and what hurts. The method is the one I always use, on steroids: create an asset, put it on a website, send a link. We will run all of it from a Web Summit newsroom of our own, with vaults to collaborate and a data feed, built like the PHP story site but simpler. And the team will learn the two agentic workflows we run today, the email workflow and the website workflow on a schedule, starting with the website one.

item.title: Feisty Duck, briefed: Ivan Ristić's cryptography and security news, newsletter, guide and history as an anchor for everything SSL, TLS and PKI, what it shares with our newsrooms, and how we could integrate with it
item.description: Feisty Duck, the small London publisher run by Jelena and Ivan Ristić since 2009, is one of the sources I trust most for anything to do with SSL, TLS, PKI and applied cryptography. Ivan wrote SSL Labs and Bulletproof TLS and PKI, and the Cryptography & Security Newsletter goes to more than 50,000 subscribers. In August it launched Feisty Duck News: it monitors 37 sources, from Adam Langley and Filippo Valsorda to Let's Encrypt and the IETF, takes reader submissions, summarises each article with an LLM, and promotes items to the front page by hand. Its feed held 100 items from 1 September to 25 October, a quarter of them on post-quantum cryptography. The rest of the site is just as useful: a free Bulletproof TLS Guide, updated in June, and an SSL/TLS and PKI history of 174 events, from SSL v2 in 1994 to 47-day certificates in 2029. Feisty Duck has believed in continuous publishing since 2009, which is what we do with versioned articles. This is a brief on what it is, a debrief against what we are building, and integration ideas: an anchor for our crypto claims, a crypto and TLS wire, provenance for the LLM summaries, and the history as a graph. A vault of its content would need its permission: its terms reserve reproduction, and its robots.txt asks crawlers to stay out of the news section.

item.title: Translate the assumption, not the vocabulary: Adelina Chalmers' five stages of a CTO's mindset, what they mean for how we brief boards on php2shell, and why a deck for every reader is communication with empathy
item.description: Adelina Chalmers posted the same platform problem answered by a CTO at five stages of an executive mindset, technologist, translator, commercial partner, value creator and trusted advisor, and only the last one gets invited into the exit conversation. I agree, and the table deserves to be read closely. The key line is this: "Notice what changes. It isn't the vocabulary. It's the assumption underneath." That is what real translation is: not putting engineering words into business words, which is stage two in the table, but starting from the other person's problem. It is exactly what we are trying to do on the PHP story site, where each of seven roles, from the executive to the engineer, gets its own first question, its own order and its own depth, and where we have just asked for a deck per reader. It is what I started exploring with The Cyber Boardroom: translating content to someone's role, focus, objectives, understanding, language and culture, even the power dynamics in the room, and how they want to consume it. With LLMs, we can now do this for every stakeholder, at scale. But the deck is still the voice of the person giving the information. Going to the receiver's pain points, in their language, is communicating with empathy, and very efficiently.

item.title: Software is now a product: what the EU's new Product Liability Directive actually says about software, SaaS and updates, how it would apply to php2shell, and the questions it leaves open
item.description: Lauren Zabierek shared a card on LinkedIn about the EU's new Product Liability Directive, 2024/2853: the 1985 directive never named software, and the new one makes it a product, subject to strict, no-fault liability that a EULA cannot waive, for products placed on the market after 9 December 2026. I asked under the post how it applies to SaaS, so I read the directive itself. Software is a product "irrespective of the mode of its supply", and the recitals name SaaS. Updates matter: a manufacturer cannot escape liability by saying the defect came later if it is due to software, an update, or a lack of updates needed to maintain safety, while the product is in its control; and an attacker's exploit does not reduce its liability. But the directive is narrower than it sounds. Only natural persons can claim, and only for death or injury, property not used only for work, or data destroyed or corrupted that is not used for work. A data leak is not on the list, and a company cannot claim for its own losses. Applied to php2shell, the PHP project is out of scope; a vendor or SaaS that leaves a known, fixed flaw unpatched and lets attackers wipe consumers' files is likely in. Patching does not bring an old product into scope, but a new one that is not patched has no defence. Here is what the articles say, and the questions they leave.

item.title: Simplified, or outsourced? A reply to Nadzeya Stalbouskaya on removing servers and databases: the risk is real, so map it, move only to real commodities, and ask who would certify what you now depend on
item.description: Under my LinkedIn comment that I run with no databases, serverless services and no server-side code of my own, Nadzeya Stalbouskaya asked a good question: removing servers and databases does not necessarily remove complexity; sometimes it just moves it into external services, APIs and dependencies we do not fully control, trading operational overhead today for dependency and lock-in tomorrow. So how do you tell genuinely simplifying an architecture from outsourcing its complexity? My answer: Nadzeya is right that there is risk, and it must be a conscious decision. The way to make it is to map it. On a Wardley map, moving a component from custom-built to commodity removes complexity only if what you move to really is a commodity. Replacing our own login with passkeys is that: a standard every major browser and platform supports, with a track record. Moving our data to object storage and static hosting is too. But moving to a young startup's service can look like a commodity on our map while, behind it, it is as messy as what we had, or worse. So you de-risk the move by choosing the commodity, and you can test which one you have by asking who would certify it, insure it, or sign a high SLA on it. Maturity and certifiability go together.

item.title: A secure rule, applied literally: how the PHP story's security agent's sound rule about scripts led the developer agent to copy the same code into every new repository, why nobody challenged it, and why the person accountable is the one who has to ask
item.description: The more complex agent workflows get, the more interesting their edge cases, and the more they need direction and someone accountable. Here is a real one from the PHP story. Its security agent set a sound rule: a page may only load scripts from its own site, which protects readers if anyone else's server is compromised. Then the designer, architect and developer agents planned the split of the site into six repositories, and the developer, starting the work, said that because of the security rule it would copy the shared code into each new site. The rule was right, and the copying followed from it. But it meant every fix applied four times, copies that drift apart, and no single source of truth: a security rule making the code less secure. Nobody challenged it, because every agent was doing its job. The good news about agents is that they can handle a lot of complexity; the bad news is the same. I caught it reading the developer's notes, and asked for one source instead: the shared code served once, at a fixed version with a published hash for every file, and the security policy widened by name to allow it. The first half of this article is the story; the second is the technical detail: Content-Security-Policy, hashes, versioned addresses, and how the fix keeps the protection.

item.title: Who creates the original? Mapping where the PHP story's data comes from, giving that map to the historian, and the places where we can make content nobody else has: our own counts, interviews and op-eds
item.description: With publishing working well, and the PHP site about to be split into six repositories, I want to start a new piece of work: a map of where the data in the story actually comes from. Who is creating original data, and who is passing it on? The site already holds the answer in raw form. Of the 418 sources it has captured, 277 are news pages, but when you count who first states each of the 107 claims, numbers and exploitation reports the site attributes, news outlets originate 5 of 146; organisations, agencies and named people originate almost all the rest, led by the PHP Foundation, Wiz, CISA and Cloudflare. The fact-check desk found claims relayed 29 times, 11 of them by the BBC. That map is a job for the historian, the agent that keeps the record and finds the pivot points, and it needs its own visualisations and data work. The second question is where we can create original content ourselves. We already do in a few places: figures we counted, a source watch that catches silent rewording, correction requests. The bigger opportunity is people: interviews with those affected, recorded by me or drafted by an agent, under the Open Security Summit banner, and op-eds from people involved, published on our site.

item.title: Agents need direction: how agent roles differ from human ones, why one focused agent can also be a developer, a designer and a data scientist, why that power has to be contained, and teams that send each other pull requests
item.description: The agents in our newsrooms are different from people in a few important ways, some good and some not. A line that keeps coming back in our own work is that agents can go in all directions, so they need direction. They can do a lot, and when they are not contained they cause damage: the technical debt that made us add a villager is a sign of it. But they have something we never had. Each agent runs on a model that can reason, learn and fetch what it needs, so a role focused on one thing also brings every other skill with it. My brief for the historian asks for a historian, and also a data scientist, a designer, a developer and an architect. That is powerful, and it has to be contained: the historian's role file lists the paths it may write, the shared files it may only append to, and what needs my go. Containing it means agents giving guidance to other agents, which gets complex fast, and that is where people come in: focus, ownership, and sometimes slowing things down. The refactoring we are doing now is cheaper because we did not automate too far. And one principle we can now scale: teams that send each other pull requests, an agent building what it needs as an explorer and handing it to the owning team, for the villagers and later the town planners to refactor or replace.

item.title: A call for help: journalists, editors, students and teachers wanted for a live newsroom run with agents, where every role should have a human, we cannot pay yet, and what we can offer instead
item.description: This is a call for help. Journalists are going through an identity crisis: they love the work, and the industry is not helping them through a massive transformation. There is a win-win here. They need to see agentic workflows doing real work, and where they add value to them; and the biggest limitation of our projects is that there are not enough humans working on them. The PHP story site shows it. Its team page lists 21 members: two humans, the editor and a project manager, and 19 roles run by agents or waiting to be filled. Every one of those roles should have a person connected to it: coordinating it, steering its agents, reviewing what they produce, and doing what only a person can, like the interviews and op-eds of the previous article. I cannot pay right now. What I can offer is coverage, exposure, credit under your own name, and a learning experience that is hard to find anywhere else. And if this generates revenue, the people in the roles are the ones who should be paid. Students and teachers are welcome too. If that is you, or someone you know, get in touch.

item.title: Monstream, briefed: continuous research streams run by AI agents, an integration API with signed webhooks, a free service from a small cryptography company, and how our newsrooms could use it, check it and contribute to it
item.description: A friend sent me Monstream, and I had not seen it. It is a service of continuous research streams: you describe a topic, it turns the description into rules (what must be there, what to skip, which sources to trust, how strict to be), and AI agents read sources around the clock and send you only what matches, with short summaries and links to the originals. Its home page said 5,258 pages had been read by its agents that day. It is run by Fair Math, a small fully homomorphic encryption company, which reportedly raised $1.4 million in early 2024; most of its 116 public streams follow cryptography, and the largest has 24 subscribers. There is no public pricing: following a stream "costs nothing extra", and the Mac app is free. What makes it interesting for us is a clean integration API: a stream per object in our own system, named by our own id, finds pushed by a signed webhook or pulled by cursor, and feedback on each find. Legally, its terms allow automated access only through the means it provides, so the API is the way in, and its summaries are written by AI and "can be incomplete or wrong", so a find is a lead, never evidence. There is no public stream on php2shell; creating one needs an account, which I have not made. This is how I would use it, check it and contribute to it.

item.title: Own the stack, and the trust: a reply to Bert Kok on who gets paid for journalism when AI sits between the newsroom and the reader, with agents that augment journalists rather than replace them, and a tour of what we have built
item.description: Bert Kok's essay for The News Stack argues that AI is separating the production of original journalism from the systems that synthesise it and own the interface, and that publishers may fund the most expensive layer and capture the least valuable. I agree with most of it, and we have been building the parts the essay describes. Its "knowledge architecture", where each story keeps which statements are facts and which are claims, where they came from, when they were checked and what has changed, is what the PHP story site does for php2shell, every claim tied to a dated, hashed capture. Its "interface as a sensor" is our feedback loop: one outside collaborator sent three rounds of ideas, and the agents turned them into working features within hours. Two additions. First, agents are not here to replace journalists. What our newsrooms are missing is more journalists, and more readers, because every human in the loop makes the system much better. Second, I disagree that publishers should not own the stack. They should, because the stack is no longer a multi-million investment: I am publishing ours as open source, and others will follow. What publishers must own above all is the reader's trust. That leads to an economic model for local and niche publishers, which I set out in a companion article, and a tour of what we have built, for readers who have not seen it.

item.title: Local trust, certified upwards: why local and niche publishers should take everything that has become commodity, certify the big outlets' stories about their patch and be paid for it, and why stories, like software, need someone to maintain them
item.description: The companion to my reply to Bert Kok. The publishers with the most to gain from AI are not the big generic ones but the local and the niche: the ones close to their readers, in their language and culture, with real expertise. They own the reader's trust, and trust is where the value is now. Such a publisher can take everything that has become commodity, the weather, sport results from official sources, the big outlets' global news, and serve it to its readers from their point of view, captured and kept current by agents. And it can certify upwards: when a big outlet runs a story about its area, the local journalists are the ones who can say whether it is right, and should be paid for saying so. A story with no local source behind it reads as a shadow, and readers will go to the source. This needs open interfaces, as the Competition and Markets Authority forced UK banks to open theirs from 2018, and it needs a map of who reports and who recycles, where a newsroom that cuts its experts shows it. Stories, like software, go off if nobody maintains them, and the same argument I made for maintainers applies to journalists: whoever does the expert work should be the one who is paid and the one who signs off.

item.title: A villager for the agents: a daily agent that does nothing but look for what to refactor and improve, because task-focused agents rarely step back, and why the PHP story's every release now rewrites two thousand files
item.description: The PHP story now has 23 agents, 12 of them on schedules, each with a good brief and each focused on its own job. That focus is also a blind spot. Agents that do a particular task rarely step back and ask how the whole could be improved, or what should be refactored. The PHP site shows the cost. Its version is stamped on every page, so every release rewrites the whole site: the last 20 releases each changed between 1,950 and 2,227 files, whatever they were for. One repository, one build, one gate and one board file serve every agent, and since 23 October 28 release messages name a conflict, a collision or a renumbering. When I asked, the dev agent proposed splitting the site into six repositories, each with its own writers, version and gate. That is a good engineering problem to have, and it is the kind of thing nobody notices while doing their own task. So I am adding a villager: an agent that runs once a day, reads what changed, asks why problems happened and where things could be better, and leaves recommendations for each agent. It does not have to act straight away. And, beside the security check every agent already does, every agent should do a quality check: a comment, not necessarily a change. The project is not ready for a town planner yet. It is ready for someone to keep an eye on quality.

item.title: The side stories of php2shell: provenance, features built against a real problem, who corrects their reporting, a crisis with no named victim, the sites that went dark, the flaws nobody watched, and how much of it was AI
item.description: The PHP story site now holds enough data to go back in time and see how php2shell evolved, and that opens up stories beyond the headline. Provenance, which almost nobody does except Wikipedia. Building features against a real problem: 179 releases in three and a half days, each answering a need, none good enough the first time, and all of it a template for the next incident and for this newsroom. Who corrects their reporting: twelve correction requests are drafted, and one publisher, Amazon, changed "broadly exploited" to "broad exploitation attempts" without a note. A crisis with no named victim, which raises three questions at once: nobody has to disclose, nobody was hit, or sites were taken down for a danger that did not come. Detection: if an attack can be counted, it can be blocked, so why so few shared rules? The 17 entries in the ledger of sites that went dark, and what that cost. Who is being paid, when nobody is exploiting it. The flaws nobody watched: Zimbra's remote code execution is on CISA's exploited list with a national CERT reporting compromises, and got 16 news items to php2shell's 175. And how much of this was AI: AI helped find the flaws, but none of the public proofs of concept VulnCheck reviewed works the way the flaw does. If AI could do what people say it can now, where is the exploitation?

item.title: Sources and their shadows: the licence, the access, the links and the quotes of every reference, how a paywalled article can be seen through what others say about it, and paying the sources we use
item.description: The PHP story is where this newsroom explores, and this newsroom is where the lessons settle: the wires here, the Industry Wire, AWS, OWASP and Portugal, will become more effective with what the PHP agents are learning. One lesson is about references. Every source a story uses comes with a set of primitives worth recording: its licence (Creative Commons, Wikipedia's share-alike, or all rights reserved), its access (open, behind a bot challenge, behind a paywall), its links, its quotes, its quality, and its history. The PHP site's source watch already records the access and keeps the history: of 913 pages it watches, 735 were open, 59 behind a bot challenge and 15 paywalled. The idea I want to explore is the shadow. When we cannot read an article, we can still read what others say about it. Wikipedia's PHP2Shell article rests 8 of its 39 statements on paywalled sources, including a quote from The New York Times, which its editors could read and we can now cite. From enough shadow you can start to see the article. You can also see where the shadow and the source disagree, and, over time, who did the research and who recycled it. And where we use a source's work, there should be a payment funnel back to it, through the micropayments our readers pay us, especially when the source certifies how we used it.

item.title: Why agent loops are hard: ten agents in sequence, a schedule that has to land in the right session, and why I spend as long making the system visible as building it
item.description: The PHP story is now run by a pipeline of agents that wake on their own: a researcher finds sources, a curator turns them into evidence, a journalist updates the site, and a correspondent checks the journalist's work; then the Sherpa, the desk, the librarian and the ontologist run after them. Eleven schedules, 53 wakes a day. It works, but it is brittle, and the reasons are worth writing down. Each agent needs its own session that I can open and read, holding its state, its keys and gigabytes of vaults between wakes. For a long time the platform's scheduling opened a new session for every run, which made secrets and state start again and the list of sessions grow with every wake. A couple of days ago I found I could schedule a wake into a specific session, and that is what made the pipeline possible; it still took a day and a half to become somewhat reliable, and this morning the wake timeline still showed 5 wakes met and 11 missed, mostly runs that worked but left no record. That is why I go slowly, use what the platform provides and keep my own code to a minimum, and spend as much time on visualisation as on the setup itself. The next step is the move from explorer to villager: a dedicated account for the whole team, for isolation and for costs, usage and models I can see. And a lesson for platform builders: the unit of work is the whole platform.

item.title: PHP October 2026, update 3: a vendor withdraws the first claim of a break-in, a third flaw, a pipeline of agents that review each other, and a control room for all of it (24 October, 23:40 UTC)
item.description: The third update on php2shell and the newsroom covering it, as of 23:40 UTC on 24 October. Three days after the release, still no organisation has said it was compromised through php2shell. The one security vendor that had claimed a successful compromise, Sophos, withdrew it; US banks and the large crypto platforms report none; and neither flaw was on CISA's exploited list. There is news on the flaw itself: on 23 October PHP published an advisory for a third, separate flaw, CVE-2026-115560, which affects fully patched releases and will be fixed in the next regular release. The newsroom changed shape. Its agents now work as a pipeline, researcher, curator, journalist, correspondent, then the graphs, where each stage reads only the one before, and the correspondent's first review caught nine things the journalist had missed, including that third flaw. A control room shows every agent at a glance. Wikipedia's PHP2Shell article is now read as a graph, with all 364 of its revisions. The site has a threat model, 40 security advisories kept like incidents, and private vulnerability reporting. And the bottleneck is still me: 16 items wait on my decisions.

item.title: Who signs for this? Accountability maps from the hardware to the business, what is measured and what is declared, and why the parts nobody signs are the blind spots worth paying to see
item.description: My article on who maintains the PHP you run argued for versions signed off by the people who maintain them. On LinkedIn, Andrey Lazarev, co-founder and CEO/CTO of TactiQ AI, took it a step further. A maintainer's signature says who stands behind a version, not whether that version is what the device actually booted. That needs a measured boot record, checked against the signed reference by someone other than the supplier. And the context of where it runs splits in two: what the device can measure itself, and what it cannot see, which has to be declared and signed by an operator or an auditor. A certificate stays honest when it keeps the two apart and names who signed each line. I think that is exactly right, and it generalises. Once people sign for what they are accountable for, they also define what they do not sign for. Map every layer, from the hardware to the business contract, and each line ends either in somebody who signed, or in a blind spot. That map is a fractal graph of signed certificates, and complexity is not the objection: how much of it you need depends on how much the application matters. The point is to make the blind spots visible, so the business and its insurers can decide whether they are comfortable with them, and so the experts who close them get paid. And when the person who signed leaves, the gap shows.

item.title: Process behaviour policies: the most locked-down Linux process we could build inside Claude's own cloud container, derived from one traced run, enforced by the kernel, for about a tenth of a second
item.description: The behaviour policy family has policies for agents, decisions, workflows, skills and applications. This one is for a process. It started with sgit and keys: we want sgit to work with PKI keys rather than holding a vault key, so the vault key has to live somewhere else, in a small process acting as a key service or a network broker. That only helps if sgit's own process cannot reach the key, which led to a bigger question. Inside a cloud container, everything runs as root, which is bad practice and no defence in depth. So what is the most locked-down process Linux lets us build there? We built it, in this newsroom's own Claude Code container, and measured it. A policy is derived from one traced run: every file the process reads, every system call it makes, every host it talks to. Then the kernel enforces it with seven walls: a user that exists for one run, an empty read-only root holding only the listed files, its own namespaces, Landlock, a seccomp allowlist, a network broker that only opens tunnels to the policy's hosts, and limits. A probe that, as root, could read /etc/shadow, the agent's home and the internet could do none of it under the policy. The cost was 92 to 187 milliseconds a run. And the size of the policy is a measure of the software: Hello World in C needs 1 file and 12 system calls; sgit needs 1,025 files and 58.

item.title: Signed by the source: asking the people and companies we quote to sign that we represent them correctly, why that is cheaper than every reader checking, and how readers go on the record too
item.description: Every article here is built on sources: papers, pages, government notices, company statements. Today, the only way to know that an article represents a source correctly is for someone downstream to check: a domain expert, or an agent with the right context, loading the article and every reference and mapping one to the other. That costs hours of human time or a lot of tokens, it is repeated by every reader, and it is done by someone who is not the best person to judge. The best person is the source. So I want to ask the people and companies we quote to review how we used their work, add a caveat where needed ("70%, but only of these"), and sign it with a key their own website vouches for. Every reader after that checks one signature and how much they trust the signer. Where an article earns money, the source should be paid to verify, as some journals now pay reviewers. Most of the pieces exist: the Pen on every article, signed notes checked against the register at pki.sgit.ai, sign in with a key, and a way for a domain to prove which key is its own. In my memo I said pki.sgit.ai's latest work was federation between organisations; it is not, and that part is still a proposal. Readers and researchers can go on the record too, with signed reviews and notes. I want to start with individuals, then companies.

item.title: Patch for breakfast: nobody refuses to patch because they want to, a patch is surgery without tests and a pipeline, and why the PHP crisis is the moment to invest in being able to change
item.description: php2shell has done something rare: it has the board's attention, and executives are asking good questions. There is some hype, but the impact is real. Nobody takes a website down lightly, and organisations took real sites down this week because they could not answer one question: are we safe? And you cannot be safe if you cannot deploy a patch. In my experience nobody fails to patch because they do not want to. The teams with the best pipelines patch for breakfast and run out of things to patch, because a patch is a change to a system, and they have the tests and the automation that make a change routine. Without them, patching is surgery: manual testing, people who could deploy long gone, side effects nobody knows. So it gets postponed, and a system that has not been updated in years is a signal of technical debt and of risk that we can measure. The PHP fix itself touched 389 files. The answer is not to patch, bring the site back and move on, because the next flaw will find it in the same state. It is to invest in the pipeline, the tests and paid maintenance, and the money being spent bringing sites back this week says the economics already add up.

item.title: A team frozen in time: agent sessions with a mandate, a role and a repository, paused and picked up again, and why that changes what happens when the people who built a system move on
item.description: Every project has a moment when the team is sharp, everyone is there, and features ship fast. Then the project dries out, the goals are met, or the company is sold, and the team moves on, taking with it the knowledge of why the system was built the way it was, its side effects, and how to build and ship it. Years later a fix is needed, as with PHP this week, and nobody can make it safely; sometimes even the pipeline is gone. I am now experiencing something we never had: agent sessions that are focused on one piece of work, with one mandate, one role and one repository, which can be paused and picked up again later, with the conversation, the reasoning, the lessons and the code exactly where they were. The best examples are the teams behind the sgit CLI and SG/Send, the vaults, which I keep coming back to: one of their sessions has resumed after 43 days without a commit, and another after 36, starting from the current code and getting straight back to tested work. On the PHP story's team, two sessions did the same this week after 28 hours. A new developer who joins such a project inherits the history, the materials, and agents ready to make the change. That is a very powerful idea, and I want to capture it.

item.title: A tangent that shipped: how sgit's pack mode went from a slow clone to a release in ten days, and took the PHP story's biggest vault from a 13-minute clone to 95 seconds the day after
item.description: This is a story about how innovation sometimes happens organically, and why I let myself go on tangents. It started with a bug: a vault that took 59 seconds to clone, measured by this newsroom, and the comms vault that took three and a half minutes. Fixing that led me to ask whether sgit could run a vault from a zip file, partly because I want vaults that live on Google Drive, Dropbox or a USB stick, with no server for us to maintain. The CLI team researched it with no code, designed a pack per push, had it reviewed four times by a second agent, and released sgit-ai 0.24.0 on 22 October. The next day, the PHP story's source watch needed it: 63,662 objects and 1.6 GB, a server that could no longer list it, a clone that took 13 minutes and 47 seconds, and one push that took 12 attempts and 2 hours 42 minutes. As a pack vault, the same history cloned in 95 seconds and pushed in 96. And it shipped without everything: the web UI still cannot open a pack vault. That was fine, because the vault that needed it did not need the UI. Small, incremental changes, done properly, made a very large difference.

item.title: A pen and a key: a place on every page to mark it, comment on it and tell the newsroom, and a browser key that pki.sgit.ai vouches for, so a note can be checked as mine
item.description: I read this newsroom on an iPad more than anywhere else, and the way I give it feedback has been a chat window and screenshots. On the page itself, selecting a sentence brings up the iPad's own Copy, Look Up and Translate menu, right where the site's Highlight button was, so the button was hidden under it. So every article now has a Pen, beside the Vault in the bar at the top. Select words and a small bar appears at the foot of the screen, away from the iPad's menu: keep them, comment on them, or tell the newsroom. The Pen opens on the right with three parts: what is selected; my marks on this page, with comments of my own that stay in my browser; and notes for the newsroom, with the passage they are about, which go when I send them, down the lane my vault already has. The fourth part is the one I care most about. pki.sgit.ai now has a register of people and their public keys, with my key as its anchor, and a rule for one key to vouch for another: an operates link, both ways, with an end date. A browser can use the same rule. The Pen makes a key for this browser with pki.sgit.ai's own code, and once my key on pki.sgit.ai says it operates that browser, every note I send from it is signed, and anyone can check it against the public register: the newsroom's lane reader does it in Python, a page does it in the browser. I looked at four ways to log in here with my pki.sgit.ai key: one passkey for both sites, a sign-in redirect like OAuth, a key per browser vouched for in the register, and the same by QR code. The key per browser works today, with nothing new on pki.sgit.ai; the redirect is the better end state; the shared passkey is a wider door than either site needs. The two vaults stay two vaults, connected by keys rather than by a shared door.

item.title: A newsroom for one: the reading list I send by email became the first page of this newsroom for the people I write to, so it now says what it is, shows what they have read, and asks for an answer
item.description: The reading list has become one of the most useful things this newsroom does for me. On 11 October I asked for a way to send someone a link that says: from me, for you, these are the articles I think you should read, in this order, and here is why. It shipped the same day. Since then the agent behind agent@riskmandate.ai has been building these lists into the emails it drafts for me, about twenty of them by its debrief of 18 October, and I read and send every one. What I had not thought through was that for most of the people I send one to, the list is the first page of this newsroom they ever open. They arrive from an email, often through a link their mail client has wrapped, and until this week they found a narrow column of titles that did not say what the site was, what a price of a few pence meant, or what to do next. So on 21 October the page changed. It now opens as a letter: a dateline, my note signed, and one line on what the list holds and what it costs. It uses the width of the screen, with the articles as cards whose pictures can be read, four more views (headlines, sections, pictures, and the list as a graph), and a column that explains the newsroom in four steps. And it shows the reader what they have read, section by section, from their own browser, with done, later and not for me on every article. Before it shipped, the newsroom's Designer role reviewed it on a real list and fourteen of its findings were fixed. This is the second page this week that had to be brought up to date because people started to use it, after the page for publishers, and it points at the next step: the answers coming back to me, and to the agent, as easily as the lists go out.

item.title: Underwriting the agent economy, reviewed: the cliff notes of the AI insurance stack, the companies already selling AI agent cover, and what agent behaviour policies add to it
item.description: In July 2026, 37 authors from insurers, brokers, universities and AI labs, led by the Artificial Intelligence Underwriting Company, published "Underwriting the Agent Economy: The Blueprint for an AI Insurance Stack". It is a thorough map of how insurance could make AI agents safe enough to adopt at scale. Its diagnosis: agent risk sits unpriced inside existing cyber and liability policies, three model providers carry over 80% of deployments, and agents' abilities double faster than actuarial tables can follow. Its proposal: eight pieces of shared industry infrastructure, from incident data to claims, with underwriting based on recurring technical tests rather than annual questionnaires, and the precedent of Underwriters Laboratories, founded by insurers in 1894. Here are its cliff notes, with screenshots and infographics, and the companies already selling AI agent cover. Then the second half: the paper is a blueprint for insurers, and it is clear about what they need from the companies they cover, who is accountable, what the agent can reach, what changed, and evidence that the controls held. It does not say how a company produces that evidence day to day. That is what we have been building at RiskMandate with agent behaviour policies, and what we built on sgit.ai with the AIUC-1 standard as a graph and insurability as a query. I map the two together, and list honestly what the paper has that we still miss.

item.title: PHP October 2026, update 2: the story held, a site that watches its own readers, agents on a schedule, and the decisions that wait on me (23 October, 23:30 UTC)
item.description: The second update on php2shell and the newsroom covering it, as of 23:30 UTC on 23 October. The story held: no named organisation has said it was breached through php2shell, CISA still lists neither flaw as exploited, and 109 of 751 affected products in the Dutch NCSC's inventory are fixed. The newsroom changed more. In a day and a half it built tools to see who reads the site and what works on it, private by design, and they found that the front page leaks: 81% of readers who start there read nothing else. An outside collaborator's five ideas turned the risk graph into a tool within hours. Scheduled agents now keep the evidence current, and our biggest data vault went from a 13-minute download to 95 seconds. And 15 of the 20 agents were waiting on a decision from me.

item.title: Almost working: a researcher, a curator and a journalist on a schedule, the QR handshake that gives each agent its key, and why a mission-critical workflow has to be built slowly
item.description: The PHP story site is now updated by three agents in a chain. A researcher follows the leads and captures pages, raw, into a large vault. A curator reads those captures and promotes what holds into a second, curated vault. A journalist reads that and updates the site, its numbers and its narrative. Each wakes on a schedule. Getting there took the better part of two days, with all the visibility and control I have, because the moment a workflow becomes mission critical every gap shows. The biggest gap was not the agents: neither Claude's scheduled tasks nor ChatGPT gives an agent an identity or a way to receive a secret. So we built one. A new agent session makes a key pair that lives only as long as the session, shows me its public key as a QR code, and I seal the vault key to it on pki.sgit.ai, signed by my root key. Then a schedule wakes that same session, which still holds the key. It is a slightly mad solution, and a lovely one. It is also not finished: on the evening of 23 October the researcher's passes are recorded, the curator has its key and its five wakes a day, and no agent has yet written its own run record. This is what it looks like to build something in its genesis stage, bit by bit, and why the next one will be much easier.
